headline: Batman vs the Lincoln Assassination: Who Wins and Why
meta_description: Batman has 30 minutes to stop Booth at Ford's Theatre. Four fights, scored F to S and checked against history. Does the plot end at the box?
dek: Batman enters Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, and fights four encounters, from a back corridor to a carriage chase, to stop Booth's conspiracy.
verdict: Batman saves Lincoln at a cost, but the wider plot keeps moving.

fights.title: The scout in the back corridors
fights.matchup: Batman vs Atzerodt's hired scout and a paid stagehand
why: The fight is decided by noise. The corridor is barely 4 feet wide and lined with scenery, so any wide swing hits a flat and brings the cast running. The grapple gun is useless in a space this tight. Batman puts the lookout stagehand down with one short strike to the hinge of the jaw. Knockouts come from rotation, not from a movie neck chop. The head snaps sideways and the lights go out.

The scout's best moment is a stage sandbag. Theaters like this flew scenery on rope with sandbags as counterweights, and a full bag is a serious weight. Swung at a man, it is a club on a rope. Batman could slip it, but slipping means stepping into the flats. So he takes it on the shoulder. Then he steps inside the arc, where the bag has no speed yet, and wraps the rope around the scout's forearm.

One pull locks the wrist and the pry bar drops. Batman catches it before it can clang and pins the scout to the wall. A joke lands on stage and the house laughs, and both men freeze until it fades. The scout gives up the name Atzerodt. In real history George Atzerodt was a German-born carriage painter who ferried Confederate agents across the Potomac. Batman ties the scout up. The costs are a bruised shoulder, a split knuckle and one stagehand who saw the cowl, with no alarm raised.

fights.title: The side exit: the silent takedown and the lantern signal
fights.matchup: Batman vs the man with the revolver and dark lantern
why: The fight has to be silent. About 1,700 people are in the building, and one gunshot or scream sends them all for the exits. Consider 1913, when a false cry of fire in a Michigan hall killed 73 people, most of them children. The armed man can't fire either, because a shot now would wreck the real plan. So he swings the lantern like a club. Batman clips its handle with a batarang and tears it out of his hand.

Batman then uses the silent takedown that Arkham players know. A blood choke squeezes the carotid arteries and takes several seconds to put someone out. Silent is slow, so Batman takes the slow, quiet option. Those seconds are long enough for the man to slam him into the edge of a stone step and drive an elbow into his side. Something in Batman's ribs gives, and he keeps the choke on.

The brick wall is why nobody upstairs hears it. It turns a fistfight into dull thumps that sound like scenery being moved. A gunshot is far louder and would get through. The man's last kick of the lantern was the signal, a burst of light thrown across the alley wall. Batman ends the fight with a cracked rib and a signal already sent.

fights.title: Batman vs John Wilkes Booth in the presidential box
why: Booth is waiting for the biggest laugh in the play. A pistol shot in a packed house needs 1,700 people roaring to cover it. Batman works that out after the side exit and takes the stairs three at a time. He reaches the door as Booth wedges it shut with a broken music stand leg. In history that bar held off rescuers. Tonight Booth gets one second to set it, which isn't enough, and Batman's shoulder knocks it away.

The box is smaller than it looks from the seats. Batman clamps both hands on Booth's wrist and drives it straight up. The gun is a Philadelphia Deringer, 6 inches long and 8 ounces, loaded from the front and firing a .44-caliber lead ball. At 4 feet, nobody dodges it. But the barrel only has to move a few degrees at the start for the ball to hit the ceiling instead of a skull. The shot goes into the plaster and Lincoln never turns around.

Booth draws a big knife. He is 5 foot 8, lean, and known for stage sword fights and acrobatic leaps. Batman pins him to the back wall because the railing is the danger. If Booth gets there, he jumps and runs. If Batman is knocked into it, the crowd sees a black shape in the box. The first slash skids off the gauntlet. The second goes above it and opens Batman's left arm, much like Booth's wound to Major Rathbone in the real history.

Batman rips a heavy curtain off its rod and throws it over the knife arm. The blade tangles, and he twists the bundle until the elbow can't follow and the knife drops. Rathbone pulls Lincoln below the railing, and nobody is hit. We put this just short of S tier because the knife drew blood. The cost was a slashed arm, one ball in the plaster, and a crowd starting to look up.

fights.title: The man behind the man: the carriage chase and the Johnson and Seward plot
fights.matchup: Batman vs the Watcher and the wider conspiracy
why: Booth tells Batman the pistol was only one piece. That links three facts: a scout who was paid and told nothing, a lantern throwing light into the alley, and an assassin saying there's more than one gun. The signal wasn't a runner's call. It was a start for whatever else happens tonight. Batman hands Booth to two army officers, tells them to get Lincoln down the back stairs, and takes Booth's own exit over the railing, a drop of about 12 feet.

He lands at about 19 mph and rolls to spread the impact. He hits the alley with one eye shut. Eyes need a long time to adapt to the dark, and light undoes that fast, so the shut eye keeps its night vision. In real history Booth's spur caught a flag on this same jump and he broke his left leg.

A galloping horse is faster than any human sprinter, and Batman has a cracked rib. Cutting each corner on the diagonal, about 30% shorter than running both sides, keeps him close for a block. It doesn't win the race. Out here there is finally room for the grapple gun. With his left arm cut he can't climb hand over hand, so the winch reels him in. He pins the Watcher and hauls back on the reins until the horse stops.

The Watcher's coat holds a wax-sealed letter in a cipher. Under the code, in plain ink, are the names Andrew Johnson and William Seward. In real history Atzerodt's job was Johnson, and he lost his nerve at a hotel bar. Seward's attacker didn't. We grade the night A overall, and the grade fits. Lincoln lives and the network has a paper trail. The plot was already moving, so A buys Batman a longer night.

takeaway: Batman wins each fight by solving the problem in front of him: noise, crowd panic, the laugh Booth planned around, and the speed of a horse. He keeps every fight quiet until the box, and in the box he wins because Booth's shot is only half a second from being aimed. Tier A means Lincoln lives and the network is exposed, but the plot against Johnson and Seward was already underway, and Batman is hurt.

notes: Draft said theaters flew scenery on hemp rope and one sandbag can weigh 50 pounds. I couldn't confirm that, so the page now says rope and a heavy bag, and the point that a sandbag is a club on a rope stays.

Draft said a blood choke takes about 9 seconds in studies of trained fighters. I couldn't confirm the figure, so it now says several seconds. The 'Nine seconds is long enough' line became 'Those seconds are long enough'.
Draft said the faster knockout in the later Arkham games is loud. I couldn't confirm that, so it was cut. Batman still takes the slow, quiet option.

Draft said walls block high pitches better and stop about 6 dB per pitch doubling, and that a gunshot is 140-165 dB. I couldn't confirm either figure, so they were cut. The page keeps the dull thumps and the point that a gunshot would get through.
Draft said the box is about 16 feet across and barely 6 feet deep. I couldn't confirm the dimensions, so they were cut. The line now reads 'smaller than it looks from the seats'.
Draft said Booth drew a Bowie-style knife. The sources I read call it a dagger and don't confirm the type, so it now says 'a big knife'.
Draft said Booth was known for balcony leaps. Sources describe acrobatic leaps on stage and skill at fencing, so it now says 'acrobatic leaps'.

Draft said historians still argue whether the jump or a later horse fall broke Booth's leg. I couldn't confirm the dispute. It now states what the sources confirm: his spur caught a flag on the jump and he broke his left leg.

Draft gave dark adaptation as 20-30 minutes and credited rhodopsin. I couldn't confirm either detail, so they were cut. The page keeps that eyes adapt slowly, light undoes it fast, and the shut eye keeps its night vision. 'rhodopsin' was removed from the entities.

Draft gave a galloping horse at 25-30 mph and the fastest human at just under 28 mph. I couldn't confirm the numbers, so the page now says a horse is faster than any human sprinter. The 19 mph landing and the 30% corner shortcut are my own arithmetic (12 ft drop; diagonal vs two sides) and stay.

Draft said investigators found a Vigenère table in Booth's hotel room. I couldn't confirm it, so the sentence and the 'Vigenère cipher' entity were removed. The wax-sealed coded letter and the names Johnson and Seward stay as the video's own story.
